European Parliament diplomacy and the end of the Cold War 
  
7 
The Minutes of a 1986 reunion of the Subcommittee on Human Rights record an exchange with 
Lorenzo Natali, Commission Vice-President, who stressed that the Commission differed in its means 
of action compared to the Parliament. The exchange suggests some tensions in the Parliament 
getting its voluminous work on human rights to the attention of the Commission. 30 In this case, the 
Vice-President, however, committed to act as an intermediary betw een the Subcommittee and 
Jacques Delors, Commission President, to enable more collaboration. 
In an interview, Jean -Pierre Cot, Chair of the Committee on Budgets from 1984 to 1989 and 
President of the Socialist Group from 1989 to 1994, stated that he experi enced the European 
Parliament's gradual rise in power during that period. He explained that it was not yet a time of co-
legislation or co -decision, but the Parliament still held, if not legal power, at least significant 
influence. He clarified that Parliament was already exerting influence on the Delors Commission. Cot 
also noted that active MEPs had this influence, and that over time, this growing impact was 
translated into the co-decision powers recognised by the Treaties.31 
Apart from seeking to benefit f rom the change to a collaborative culture brought by the Delors 
Commission, the European Parliament also used the institutional context created outside the EC to 
influence political and social outcomes in CEE. The members of the Subcommittee on Human Rights 
pursued direct contact with eastern European countries through the early mechanisms that the 
European Political Co-operation (EPC) and the Conference for Security and Cooperation in Europe 
(CSCE) offered. The CSCE conferences continued the Helsinki process between 1977 and 1989, and 
the MEPs strived to have their human rights agenda represented in the meetings that the EPC would 
hold with national delegations from eastern Europe. 
However, not all groups saw the urgency in confronting the Soviet Union with the fact that there can 
be no cooperation and security in Europe without the protection of human rights in the east. In one 
1980 debate, the difference between parliamentarians' views on how to approach the upcoming 
CSCE Madrid Conference are notable. Gér ard Israël, speaking on behalf of the Group of European 
Progressive Democrats, expressed concern over the potential failure of the Madrid Conference, 
warning that such an outcome could lead to serious repercussions, particularly in eastern Europe, 
where countries might resort to familiar repressive measures, especially regarding the situation in 
Poland. In contrast, Jacques Denis, represe nting the Communist and Allies G roup, spoke against 
urgency in dealing with this matter and was optimistic about the conference's progress, highlighting 
the strength of détente and cooperation despite initial challenges. He reject ed the idea of a return 
to Cold War attitudes and criticis ed any confrontational approach coming from what he s aw as 
'NATO hawks', emphasising a co operative rather than confrontational path. 32 In this period, the 
Group of the European Right focuse d on the rights and freedoms of nations and individuals and 
pressed for the exposure of Gorbachev to demands for free elections in the countries of the east.33 
It is not until 1987 that the EPC presidency agrees to receive a delegation of the European Parliament 
under its umbrella and support MEPs' contacts with delegates from eastern Europe, yet without 
being allowed to attend plenary sessions or participate i n negotiations. For the 1987 CSCE 
Conference to be held in Vienna, the Subcommittee on Human Rights prepared a dossier of 
                                                        
30 Minutes of the Meeting of the Subcommittee on Human Rights  (28 February 1986), Historical Archives  of the 
European Union (HAEU), PE2-1579//PE2 AP PV/POLI.1984 SCDH-19860228.  
31 Interview with Jean-Pierre Cot, 28.05.2018 (Gerard Laprat), EUI Oral History Collections, Historical Archives of the 
European Union (HAEU), INT817-A.1 
32 Conference on Security and C ooperation in Europe  (19 November 1980), Debates of the European Parliament, 
Historical Archives of the European Union (HAEU), PE1.AP.DE.1980//DE19801119-05/0010. 
33 Motion for a resolution on a Statement by the European Community to mark the visit to France by Mr. Gorbachev  
(9 September 1985), Historical Archives of the European Union (HAEU), PE2.AP.PR.1985//B2-0839/85/0010.
